entries.title: The Best Popular Science Books of 2026: The Royal Society Book Prize, recommended by Michael Benton
entries.summary: The Royal Society celebrates the best new popular science writing every year through the prestigious Trivedi Science Book Prize. entries.content:
The Royal Society celebrates the best new popular science writing every year through the prestigious Trivedi Science Book Prize. We asked Professor Michael Benton, the eminent palaeontologist and chair of the 2026 judging panel, to talk us through their six-book shortlist: from a globe-trotting history of alchemy to a fast-paced account of memory manipulation by optogenetics researchers at the cutting edge of science.

You chaired the judges of the Royal Society’s Trivedi Science Book Prize. What were you looking for when you were looking for the best popular science books of the last twelve months?

We’re looking for books that convey the excitement and the fun of modern science. They have to be accessible to the general reader, of course, so we look at the assumptions being made by the authors and the language they use to explain things. We exclude books aimed at the specialist scientist or people working in the field.

We’re looking for accuracy, of course. The books need to give a correct presentation of the subject matter, and be therefore written by people in the field or journalists who do good research. They have to be original. If there are dozens of titles on the same subject already available – as there are, for example, on understanding evolution, or the great unsolved mathematical mysteries, or how modern medicine is helping people live longer – that raises the question of novelty.

Our definition of ‘science’ is quite broad. The competition has always been open to core science like physics, chemistry, biology, mathematics. But it is also open to medicine and engineering and the history of science. So there is a wide scope. That does mean we get a very large number of books being submitted for consideration.

I think that’s it: accessibility, novelty, plausibility, and accuracy.

You mentioned history of science. That leads us to our discussion of this year’s winner of the Royal Society’s Trivedi Science Book Prize, which is The Age of Alchemy: How Early Innovators Shaped Modern Chemistry. I’d love to hear what the judges enjoyed and admired about this book.

I think everybody on the committee was pleasantly surprised by this book. At first, we thought this was a topic about which many books have been written before. Look up any bookseller’s website and you will find a number of books with the words ‘alchemy’ and ‘chemistry’ in the title. But what we all found exciting about this book was that the storytelling is superb. It moves along at a good pace, you’re engaged and drawn in.

Each chapter tells a story of particular historical figures. Many of them are untold stories. That was the second thing we liked – it doesn’t tread the normal ground. There have been many histories of chemistry, with a focus either on the history itself or by explaining chemistry through the history of its development. But many of them start only 300 or 400 years ago, with the discovery of oxygen, or something like it – Lavoisier in France and Priestley in England.

Kit Chapman starts long, long before, in the days of ancient Egypt and biblical times in the Middle East and in ancient China. So he’s delving deep. You go through half the book before you come across a modern European scientist. This point is a strong one – we felt he was doing the difficult stuff, going deeper into time, to where people were not documenting their work, not writing scientific papers.

We liked the democratic aspect of the book. In those ancient times, people trying to do or understand chemistry were practical people doing it for practical reasons. For them, it was all about understanding how to cook things, how to make food, how to modify food, how to tan leather, or how to make metals of different kinds. People discovered the practical properties of iron and brass and bronze and other useful things. So much of it was utilitarian and the people are not named individuals, but we know of them from ancient documents. That’s wonderfully well told.

The Royal Society is always very keen to internationalise as well – this is not the European white man history that we are used to hearing about. This is women, slaves, people without a voice. They were the ones who were discovering stuff in those early days.

And the alchemy element is the fun stuff. In his acceptance speech, Kit Chapman talked about one of the common features of many chapters in the book, which is what you can make of urine. You can tan leather with it, do all kinds of stuff. They also though they could make gold or other valuable metals out of urine, so they spent a lot of time collecting human and sheep and cow and horse urine, distilling it, trying to get something out of it, and of course they largely failed. Nonetheless, that’s all part of the quest.

So it’s good fun, it’s novel, it’s credible – Kit Chapman is a chemist who knows his stuff. But most readers will simply enjoy it as a rattling good read, and at the end of that they will think: Wow, I enjoyed that and I’ve learned something.

I see Chapman described on the blurb as “a science adventurer”. Where does that come from?

He could have sat in his study in England writing a book, painting a picture from the existing literature. But he actually goes to many of the places he talks about. We see him in the marketplace in Cairo imagining what it was like 2000 years before, with all the noise and the hustle of the crowds. He went off to Indonesia the day after he won the prize. I think the travel is part of what he’s doing – he speaks to people, tries to get that global aspect of his subject matter, to avoid the risk of retreading old ground.

You know, there must be a thousand books about Darwin, a thousand books about Newton, so there’s always the question: is there anything new in here, or are you recycling the same old stuff? You may be a great stylist, you may be writing it in a bright and sparkling way, but you can still be recycling. Whereas Kit Chapman is forcing himself into these other cultures, speaking to people and gathering information. A lot of what you read here will not be found in other books about chemistry or history.

Let me say first, in general terms, that all of the shortlisted six were unanimously found by the whole committee to be fantastic. When we turned up for the final discussion and decision, there was no way to tell in advance which would be the winner. Each of us had read them all and had our own opinions, but we deliberately didn’t compare notes before the meeting.

I invited each of the members of the committee to speak freely and to tell us what they thought without yet voting, to say what they each thought about each of the six books.

Now, Bad Influence is a book on an important topic: it’s about misinformation, conspiracy theories, all things in constant consideration by thinking people. We have the wonderful example in the United States at the moment, where the Secretary of Health encourages this kind of nonsense.

Deborah Cohen is a very skilled journalist, this is very deeply researched, and every chapter covers a different topic, a different disease, or a different therapy. It includes things like plastic surgery and other medically related themes. There’s also a bit of history of the opioid crisis, although that’s been written about before.

So it is hugely timely. It’s well researched, and has huge importance for the current understanding of and thinking about the future. How do we, in a world of infinite knowledge and exchange of information by way of the internet, communicate and help people to recognise good information from bad? That’s what Deborah Cohen achieves and it’s a great contribution to the field of social medicine and ways for medical researchers to communicate and understand responses.

Fred Pearce is a journalist of great renown. He’s written many books and many articles for New Scientist and other places. He has spent his life writing about the climate crisis, which is another of these enormous topics equally full of misunderstanding and misapprehension. He doesn’t talk about conspiracy theories the way Deborah Cohen does, but the world does need sober and sensible information on this topic; otherwise, people do get misled by incredible nonsense online.

Fred Pearce has written all about climate change from inside different branches of science. He has seen the worst of it. He’s seen the appalling damage of stripping away tropical rainforests, excessive agriculture, excessive carbon dioxide from polluting factories and cars and aircraft. But here he is actually looking for hope and he sees that some things are good.

Renewable energies – solar and wind – might not be coming in fast enough, but they are really happening. This has come in in our lifetimes. He looks at the biodiversity crisis and finds bright lights of hope here and there. People are paying attention, and in some places they are no longer cutting down forests. They are reversing it.

Some books about the climate crisis are overly gung-ho, sometimes for political reasons – they argue that there is no crisis, that everything is fine. Fred Pearce is not like that. He’s writing from a position of full understanding of the chemistry, the biology, and other aspects of science that are part of the debate. And I think it is really helpful.

Simply being a doom-monger doesn’t always get people’s attention. Saying: there are some bright lights, and if we follow these examples we can dig ourselves out of a hole might.

Again, it’s brilliantly written. It’s a nice, short book. Both Fred Pearce and Deborah Cohen are wonderful science journalists who produced great books that were very strong contenders.

Here’s a book with a very strong human dimension – how we exploit nature, in this case fish. Rose George has written books before about aspects of the ocean.

Yes, and other people have written on fisheries and fishing before. But I think Rose George makes each chapter a personal story. She’s been out on fishing boats from European, North American, African ports. She’s been out to sea with marine conservationists. She’s talked to people in navies and regulatory bodies. There are bits of history here and there about how the fishing industry has changed. She even spends a shift in a fish and chip shop talking to the people there about what they are selling as cod and haddock – and what these fish portions really are.

So, a personal book written from her own experiences. I don’t think she had a long-time involvement in the field, but it was something she decided to investigate. And it’s beautifully written and makes you think.

I don’t think she eats fish herself.

Yes, she says at the start that she’s a vegan. That made me wonder, at first, that she might not be the right person to write on this topic. But it doesn’t intrude, other than the personal remark that she’s looking at this subject in a dispassionate way, on the understanding that other people do want to eat fish – and what does that mean?

Many fish-eaters don’t think much about the detail of where it comes from and what damage is being done. We might read about these things, but it’s usually in a European context. Rose George ventures much further afield and she looks sympathetically at the people who have to catch fish for a living. It’s not all about the big industry end of things, but also the processing and how the fish goes from the sea eventually into the supermarket. This diversity of topics is probably greater than most readers would have expected and the depth of presentation of each is very engaging. It’s thoroughly referenced throughout, and it’s a novel, storytelling book that holds the attention.

There is a shift in science writing more generally, I think – towards first-person storytelling, bringing in that personal strand. Did you notice that too?

I think you’re right. At one time, people would have thought it improper. That they are here to deliver facts. It’s true that we exclude textbooks and field guides from this prize, so we don’t include certain kinds of work that also deserve attention and admiration, because no less effort goes into those. But I think you are right, it’s a common thread in the books that we were looking at.

You’re right. This book is talking about an area of biology that will change our understanding of medicine and ourselves. I knew nothing about microchimerism before reading this book. And we also had another interesting question with this, which is that it is a translation so how far should we go in being swayed by the styling. In the end, we decided just to treat it as any other book, without inquiring too much about what belongs to the author and what to the translator. And it’s great.

Lise Barnéoud also involves herself in the story. She is a journalist but has spoken to many of the key scientists in the field, visiting them in their labs, Zooming them, and giving personal reflections from those scientists – how excited they were when they made discoveries.

This is very much at the frontline of science, the latest news. She’s talking about work published early in 2026, so this is a fast-moving field.

It’s also a topic that could seem very abstruse, but she gets the message across clearly: Do you realise your genome is not just yours as an individual? You have samples of the genomes of a lot of other people residing permanently within you, and, good grief, that’s a scary thing. What does that mean? I’ve got no idea, but it’s a fact, and she describes very clearly how the maternal genome is inserted into the offspring, not only in the obvious way through the egg, but in other ways, and equally there is back-influencing from the embryo to the mother which was entirely unexpected. There’s also sampling of genomes between siblings. So there’s a shock aspect, and she tells the science in an accessible way that makes it really clear.

Four of our shortlisted books were written by science journalists, and two of them by scientists. They are all reading original papers, speaking to involved scientists, and sometimes – as with Rose George – even going out on trawlers, getting seasick, and all sorts of stuff.

With microchimerism, it’s an ongoing story and I imagine that Lise will write another version in ten years with many more chapters and more understanding of what it all means, if anything, to the way that we function. It’s a wonderful book.

Really fascinating. And it brings us to our final book on the shortlist for the Royal Society Trivedi Science Book Prize, which is How to Change a Memory: A Quest to Alter the Past by Steve Ramirez, a MIT neuroscientist who specialises in a field called optogenetics. What an intriguing title.

There’s real timeliness here, because the Nobel Prize in Chemistry has just been awarded to the three people who originally discovered this effect – that you can study the cells of the brain by illuminating them brightly with lights. When we met him last week, Ramirez had no inkling that would happen.

So, it is a scientist writing about his own quest. He’s quite a young man, barely over 40, and he’s able to take you right to the lab bench and to talk you through the mechanics of the process of being a scientist in a forefront area like this. The practicalities: How do you get permission to do experiments on animals? How do you make sure those experiments are not distressing for the animals? How do you fund your work? How do you publish your papers? How do you get grants? This is the only book in the collection that has that component.

Like the microchimerism book, How to Change a Memory is science on the hoof. It’s really moving fast, and I imagine Steve already wants to write another three chapters to bring us up to date. It’s very much a personal story, and it’s written in a very lively style, presenting the helter-skelter of fast-moving science.

He had a very strong relationship with another scientist, who sadly died, and he documents that – the devastation of the death of his collaborator – and how he went on to continue the work, and get to the point he has got to.

It is a remarkable thing, to be able to say that you can take a brain and alter its memory. That you can go in and remove a sad memory, or remove the feeling of unhappiness, and make a person happy. Or, a rat, at least. But how far you go with that, I just don’t know. I’d love to hear what the philosophers have to say.

It’s a remarkable quest in science, part of which – the work of Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel – has been validated by the Nobel Prize. It’s lively, fascinating, engaging – and I’m sure it will sell well and deservedly so.

Thank you. Listen, that brings us to the end of the list. I wondered if I could finish by asking if the process of judging has left you feeling optimistic about the state of science writing today?

I think it has. There was a measure of pessimism in the fact that, at an early stage, we had to weed out a number of AI-produced books. I do think that the influence of AI and automated book production will get more substantial. If you look at Amazon, you can buy any number of cheap books cobbled together from Wikipedia. Initially this was done by hand, from online stuff. Now you don’t even need to write them yourself. So that’s a pity.

But once we got down from the initial 200 to a longlist of 40, it became very heartening. These were all really, really good books. All excellent in their field. That there were so many in the English language and available – well, it was good.

We were looking at them quite seriously because the panel involved a number of people who make their living from writing and selling books, very much in the field, and they all expressed themselves happy. The difficulty we had in deciding the winner also illustrated that fact.

In some ways it would be wonderful if there were more science book prizes. There aren’t many in the world, and although we think of the Royal Society’s as a British competition, many outside the country see it as a somewhat international one, because of the scale of the prize and the publicity and the impact on sales. So, it’s a great thing. Long live the Royal Society Trivedi Science Book Prize.

Michael Benton

Michael Benton is a palaeontologist who has made fundamental contributions to understanding the history of life, particularly concerning how biodiversity changes through time. Michael has written engaging books for children on the theme of dinosaurs, as well as a significant number of palaeontology text books for university students. He founded the MSc in Palaeobiology at Bristol in 1996, from which more than 450 students have graduated. He has supervised more than 75 PhD students.

entries.title: The Best Adventure Novels: The 2026 Wilbur Smith Prize, recommended by Alex Bescoby
entries.summary: What makes a great adventure novel? For Alex Bescoby, filmmaker, traveller and judge of the 2026 Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize, it’s the ability to transport readers to unfamiliar worlds and bring history vividly to life. Here, he discusses the six shortlisted novels, from ancient Britain to revolutionary India, exploring stories of endurance, rebellion and remarkable perseverance in the fa
entries.content:
You’re one of the judges of this year’s Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize. Before we get to the books that have been shortlisted, can you tell us a bit about your qualifications as an adventurer?

I’m a professional traveller and filmmaker. I tell stories from faraway places. The projects I do are through a company called Grammar Productions, and what unites them is travel and history—a journey with a pedigree of some sort. I’ve worked across five continents and done all sorts of things, but I guess I’m probably best known for a series called The Last Overland and the book that I wrote about that. It was about a journey from Singapore to London in a 1950s Land Rover. It was recreating a journey from the 1995-6, called the First Overland.

I now run a production company that sends people all over the world doing great journeys with great stories behind them.

And is there always a lot of history involved?

I studied history, and it’s my favourite subject. It gives any journey, in the present day, a greater meaning if you are investigating something that went before, whether that’s following in the footsteps of an author that’s been dead for centuries, or going in search of a lost civilization, or just going to the end of the lane with your daughter. It’s trying to learn something about why the world is the way it is that makes a journey worthwhile.

In terms of the books on the 2026 adventure writing shortlist, what qualities were you looking for when you were deciding which one should be the winner?

I’m a nonfiction travel writer, which is easy because you’re going from A to B.  You maybe have to find a narrative around it, but you’re basically dealing with something that’s happened. Whereas I admire anyone who writes fiction because you’ve got this infinite universe of possibility, and you’ve got to make it work.

The lens I applied when judging was, ‘Does this take me on a journey where I learn about a part of the world or a period of history—or both—that I had no idea about, and do it in a way that didn’t feel like homework?’ If I’m going to dedicate my time to a book, I want to come away having learnt about a place or a person. I love historical fiction or anything that takes its leap from real people and real places. That really inspires me.

My favourite book of all time is The Glass Palace by Amitav Ghosh. It’s the book that started my career. I knew nothing about Southeast Asia. It was a book that was so well written that not only did I leave it feeling like I could enter that world for a bit, I then decided to dedicate my whole academic and professional life to it for about 10 years.

That’s what I’m looking for.

Let’s turn to the books that made the shortlist of the 2026 Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize. First up is The Tarot Reader of Versailles by Anya Bergman. So this is historical fiction with fantastical elements, but based on a true story. Tell me about it and why you liked it.

This is the book I wanted to pick up first, just because I have a soft spot for the French Revolution. The Ancien Régime and the 18th century is just a fascinating period of French history. It’s about a character who I now know was real, but I’d never heard of. I enjoyed the book because the historical setting was something I’d spent a lot of time reading about, but the story was told through the eyes of a character that I didn’t know existed. It was just a really enjoyable romp.

And the main character was a tarot reader?

Yes, you get them today. She was the celebrity shaman of the day. She was reading the fortunes of the great and good in the midst of this time of complete turbulence, and—whether it’s true or not—having an impact on the way that events are unfolding. That mixture of realpolitik and superstition and fortune-telling—I loved it.

Let’s go to the next book, which is set in late Iron Age or early Roman Britain. This is Boudicca’s Daughter by Elodie Harper.

I have a real soft spot for Boudicca. There’s a massive statue of her on Westminster Bridge in London. The Victorians loved Boudicca. She was seen as an ancient British rebel against the Romans, which is weird because she’s from a completely alien culture to what we consider as England from Alfred the Great onwards. She was part of a culture and with a language that we wouldn’t recognise today, but she’s embraced as this national hero.

I also love reading about Dark Age Britain—I’m a huge Bernard Cornwell fan.

The only thing I knew about Boudicca’s daughters was that they were raped. That was the inciting incident for Boudicca’s revolt. They’re never named, and you never hear anything about their story in the sources.

What I really loved about this book is that it brought to life somebody who was just a footnote. It builds a whole world and a life for this person we know nothing about. It’s done in such a way that, as long as you accept that it’s fiction, it was a really good way of trying to step into the shoes of someone who has found themselves on the edge of two worlds.

And is it a realistic kind of depiction of that world, do you think?

I mean, as much as we can be realistic about a culture that was essentially eradicated and happened a very long time ago. There’s not a lot to work from, but I found the story compelling.

Let’s go on to Esperance by Adam Oyebanji. What was this one about?

This was probably the most ambitious book on the shortlist. It’s really unique. It mixed murder mystery, sci-fi and the slave trade. The author is a fascinating man whose day job is exposing financial terrorism and sanctions evasion and investigating high financial crime.

The book starts off with this mad, impossible murder and takes you on this journey. What I loved about it was that it taught me aspects of the history of the slave trade that I wasn’t aware of. So that was very interesting.

Is it set in the present or in the past?

A mix.

Next we have The Fertile Earth by Ruthvika Rao. This was the winner of this year’s Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize—please tell me why it’s such a great book.

I knew it was the winner from the moment I started reading it. It follows a family over time. It’s quite similar to The Glass Palace in that it takes place across several decades in India, although 100 years or so later. It’s set in post-independence India, in the 1960s and 70s, during the Naxalite uprisings around Hyderabad. I’ve read a lot of Southeast Asian history, but I never knew much about the Naxalites. Now I understand who they were and what they were trying to do.

The writing is exquisite, and you wouldn’t need to know or care about India in the 1960s and 70s to find this book unbelievably moving. I’ve worked a lot in India, so when she’s describing the colours and smells—which she does amazingly—I think, ‘I’ve been to places like that. I know what that thing she’s describing smells like. I know what that tree looks like. I know what the dress she’s talking about looks like.’

It sounds amazing.

It’s one of those books that I was literally finishing it at seven in the morning. My daughter woke up and she was crawling all over me, but I just carried on reading to the end.

And what was the Naxalite uprising about? What was the cause of it?

It was a dismantling of the Raj, but also of a system that was much, much older than that—a feudal system where you had the landowners overseeing an indebted, indentured servitude. They had generational farming families and the landowner in the grand house in the middle. It was a form of modern slavery, where families were expected to send workers to the house for free.

It tells the story from both sides. It tells it from the perspective of the landowners, this class of privileged Indians in a world that’s falling apart, but it also tells it from the Naxalite point of view. It shows why people joined this incredibly ruthless, brutal, bloody, murderous campaign to dismantle the feudal system. It’s horrific. It starts off with a horrific mass murder and ends by going back to it again.

The next book takes us to 1920s London. This is Poor Girls by Clare Whitfield.

This one’s great fun. It’s a story about 1920s gang culture, with female protagonists. It’s really well written, and it’s pacy, and the characters are great. The question we asked ourselves as judges is, ‘What counts as an adventure?” This is not the classic Joseph Campbell hero’s journey, necessarily. No one goes on a great adventure and comes back. But there is an adventure here. A woman breaks out of her life and enters a life of crime and has an adventure along the way.

Having spoken to judges of the prize in previous years, my feeling is that the Wilbur Smith Prize is trying to broaden the definition of an adventure.

Yes, my own book The Last Overland is more the standard formula of the hero’s journey—someone feeling the call of adventure, and going out and documenting their own change across six months.

In these books, you’re following a character across time, and it is an adventure. There’s endurance, there’s rebellion, there’s amazing perseverance in the face of hardship. In each of these books, you will find a character that is inspiring—someone who spurs you to go out and see more of the world and do something you didn’t think you could do beforehand.

And last but not least on the shortlist we have White Road, an eco-thriller set on an Arctic oil rig by Harry Whitehead. What’s this one about?

It’s just a cracking murder mystery adventure, and really well written. I actually started out in the oil industry; it was my very first job. I never worked on a rig—and certainly not an Arctic one—but I know the kind of characters in that industry. I know how hard a life it is, and the strange people that it attracts.

It’s a great read. It really transports you into that world. Interestingly, a lady came up to me at the prize event. We were talking about the book, and she said, ‘I’m from the high Canadian Arctic, and I was amazed at how somebody from Scotland had written it so well.’ So that’s not praise coming from me, but from someone from northern Canada, which speaks well of Harry’s research.

I’ve seen it described as part oil rig drama, part survival story. Does that sound right?

Yes, it does. And with a bit of a ghost story in the middle of it as well, which is nice.

entries.title: Biographies for Kids
entries.summary: Biographies are a great way for kids to feel inspired by people who have achieved extraordinary things. And by enabling children to see the world through other people’s eyes, biographies can introduce them to different times and places, helping to broaden their perspectives. Here is a selection of biographies for kids that have been recommended on Five Books. This interview appeared first on Five
entries.content:
Biographies are a great way for kids to feel inspired by people who have achieved extraordinary things. And by enabling children to see the world through other people’s eyes, biographies can introduce them to different times and places, helping to broaden their perspectives. Here is a selection of biographies for kids that have been recommended on Five Books.

Biographies not only introduce kids to inspirational role models, but can teach them important life lessons. Through the stories of real individuals, children learn about the different values that drive people, and that success is usually preceded by obstacles and setbacks. Biographies can also be a good way to teach empathy and self-awareness, as young readers get glimpses of lives that are very different from their own.

Picture books for young readers that have been recommended on Five Books include gorgeous biographies of 13th century poet and scholar Rumi, and contemporary musician Evelyn Glennie.

If you are after longer picture books (over 40 pages) for slightly older readers, recommendations include Voice of Freedom about Civil Rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer, The People’s Painter about the life and work of Benjamin Shahn, I Dissent about US Supreme Court justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and The Fire of Stars, which is a brilliant combination of biography for children about astrophysicist Cecilia Payne and the birth of a star.

Josephine: A Dazzling Life is about the extraordinary life of 20th century icon Josephine Baker. It is a longer book at around a hundred pages, and is an easy, fully illustrated read to fascinate children and adults alike.

Publisher Barrington Stoke specialises in dyslexia-friendly books designed to be both interesting, quick reads for confident readers as well as accessible stories for those who find reading more challenging. That includes some excellent biographical fiction for kids, such as Journey Back to Freedom about the early life of Olaudah Equiano, Elisabeth and the Box of Colours about Élisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun (said to be Queen Marie Antoinette’s favourite portrait artist), and Respect! about the Black English professional footballer and World War 1 British army officer Walter Tull.

Continuing with recommendations for the 8-12 age range, librarian Alison King recommends the multi award-winning graphic novel The Bird in Me Flies, inspired by the life of Swedish artist Berta Hansson.

Finally, another biography with amazing artwork is the story of 17th century scientist Maria Sibylla Merian; this is surely one of the most beautifully illustrated biographies for kids ever, featuring as it does her own nature drawings.
